targets.title: The lexical statistics of word recognition problems caused by L2 phonetic confusion.
targets.evidence_quote: The current study builds on Cutler's (2005) work by examining how misperception can affect the structure of the L2 English mental lexicon. In simulating the L2 mental lexicon, a database like CELEX (Baayen et. al, 1996) is too large -it would only work for people with extremely large vocabularies. Even using the CLEARPOND (Marian et al., 2012) or KU Similarity Neighborhood calculator (Vitevitch, n.d.) for L2 learners may not be ideal, because these databases reflect the average L1 speaker's mental lexicon. Instead, we perform Cutler's three analyses using a database we built to reflect the average L2 mental lexicon: the English Vocabulary Profile Phonological database (EVP-Phon; see Methods).
targets.outcome_quote: The current study examined how misperception could affect the structure of the L2 English mental lexicon. Using a database built to simulate the size of the L2 English mental lexicon, we found larger counts of both pseudo-homophones and pseudo-phonological neighbors for /l/-/r/ misperception than /ɛ/-/ae/. Compared to Cutler (2005), we found fewer pseudo-homophones in terms of raw numbers, but a larger proportion of the L2 lexicon becomes homophonous for each misperception pattern.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Original finding stated in introduction: more pseudo-homophones from l/r than vowel confusion. Corresponding result agrees. Different raw totals and proportions arise in a deliberately smaller corpus; not treated as failed tests. No overall replication verdict; interpretation uncertain because authors also discuss changed counting conventions.
